q1.attribution: —Historian's account of absolutism under Louis XIV of France, 1661–1715
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE method Louis XIV used to strengthen royal authority.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the growth of absolutist monarchy in seventeenth-century Europe.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity in the limits on royal power between medieval and absolutist France.

sample_answers.a: He forced the high nobility to live at Versailles as courtiers, where competition for royal favor replaced their old role as independent regional powers with their own armies and clients.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the chaos of the religious wars and the Fronde, which convinced many French elites that only a strong centralized monarchy could guarantee order — combined with new tax revenues that funded standing armies loyal to the crown.
sample_answers.c: Even 'absolute' kings could not simply command revenue into existence: like medieval kings, Louis depended on the cooperation of local officeholders and faced resistance, including revolts, when taxation pressed too hard, so bargaining with elites continued.

q1.stimulus: Louis XIV made the French monarchy the model of absolutism: he required the nobility to attend him at Versailles, where court ritual replaced their independent power bases; he revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, imposing religious uniformity; and he built Europe's largest standing army. Yet his 'absolute' power had hard limits — he could not tax without provoking resistance, could not rule the provinces without intendants who bargained with local elites, and died leaving a state nearly bankrupt from war.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, bishop and tutor to the French dauphin, Politics Drawn from the Very Words of Holy Scripture, 1709
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Bossuet makes about the source of royal authority.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the passage was useful to Louis XIV's government.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between Bossuet's justification of monarchy and the Confucian justification of imperial rule in China.

sample_answers.a: He claims kings receive their authority directly from God, are God's image on earth, and answer to God alone — not to the people or the nobility.
sample_answers.b: The doctrine gave Louis's centralization a sacred cover: opponents of royal policy could be painted as opposing God's order, and the clergy were enlisted as allies of the crown.
sample_answers.c: Confucian theory made the emperor's legitimacy conditional on virtuous rule through the Mandate of Heaven, which could be lost by misrule and justify rebellion; Bossuet's doctrine offered no such conditionality — the king answered only to God.

q2.stimulus: It is God who establishes kings. They are His ministers on earth, and His image. Royal power is absolute, for the king answers to God alone; yet it is not arbitrary, for God commands kings to rule with justice.

q3.attribution: Photograph of the Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the Hall of Mirrors shown in the image.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the palace of Versailles served Louis XIV's political goals.
parts.c: Explain ONE change in the relationship between European monarchs and their nobilities between 1500 and 1700 illustrated by Versailles.

sample_answers.a: The image shows an enormously long gallery lined with mirrors reflecting light from tall windows, decorated with paintings of Louis's military triumphs — an overwhelming display of wealth and royal glory.
sample_answers.b: By housing the nobility at Versailles and making access to the king the path to favor, Louis turned potential rivals into dependent courtiers and made the monarchy the visible center of French life.
sample_answers.c: Where sixteenth-century nobles still raised their own armies and defied kings in civil wars, by 1700 the French nobility had been domesticated into courtiers whose status depended on royal favor — a shift from independent magnates to servants of the crown.

q3.stimulus: Photograph of the Hall of Mirrors in the Palace of Versailles, built under Louis XIV in the 1680s: a 73-meter gallery of mirrors, chandeliers, and ceiling paintings celebrating the king's victories.
